name: Peptide YY

lead: Peptide YY is a hormone your gut releases after you eat, signalling fullness. The 2002 and 2003 studies that showed it cut food intake sparked interest in using it for weight control.
It remains a research compound. Human studies are small and short, and no PYY product is approved for weight loss.

paras: The active form, PYY(3-36), binds Y2 receptors, including on appetite-regulating neurons in the hypothalamus, and also slows stomach emptying. Levels rise with meals, especially protein-rich ones.
Published material here does not detail safety outcomes of PYY analogues; research use is investigational and no regulatory approval for weight management exists.

lead: Peptide YY (PYY) is a 36-amino-acid gut hormone released by L-cells in the ileum and colon after eating. It acts to reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying, and it belongs to the neuropeptide Y family [1][2]. The main circulating form, PYY(3-36), acts largely through the Y2 receptor [3][2].

In 2002, researchers reported in Nature that peripheral injection of PYY(3-36) reduced food intake in rodents and in human volunteers, which led to interest in it as an anti-obesity agent [4]. It is not an approved drug for weight management or appearance. Research is described as investigational, with some small human infusion studies and an oral/lingual delivery trial registered [2][5].
infobox: Research only; no approved PYY drug

paras: PYY is secreted after meals in proportion to calorie content, and levels fall during fasting [4][2]. The enzyme DPP-4 converts PYY(1-36) to PYY(3-36), the predominant circulating form, which is highly selective for the Y2 receptor [2][6]. Protein intake is reported to raise PYY levels [2]. PYY also slows gastric emptying and promotes water and electrolyte absorption in the colon [2].

Obese people have been reported to secrete less PYY after a meal, though some studies find they remain sensitive to its appetite-reducing effect, so reduced sensitivity is not considered established as a cause of obesity [2]. After bariatric surgery, gut hormone profiles, including PYY, shift toward an appetite-suppressing pattern [7]. A study of people on a diet-induced weight-loss programme reported long-lasting hormonal changes, including altered gut hormones, after weight loss [8].

Kazuhiko Tatemoto isolated PYY in 1982 as a candidate gut hormone, and its distribution and release in humans were described in 1985 [9][2]. Its structural similarity to neuropeptide Y was noted in the same period [1][10]. A 2002 Nature paper by Batterham and colleagues reported that PYY(3-36) inhibited food intake [4], and a 2003 NEJM study reported that infusion cut calorie intake at a buffet meal by roughly 30% in obese and lean subjects [2].

Beyond injected PYY analogues, researchers have examined indirect approaches. A trial of targeted colonic delivery of propionate, a short-chain fatty acid, in overweight adults measured effects on PYY and GLP-1 release, appetite and weight gain [11]. Gut microbiota that ferment fibre are also discussed as influencing gut hormone secretion [6]. Gut hormones including PYY are covered among the incretin and related hormones in a 2018 review [12].

Human studies are small. Registered investigations include PYY infusion studies in obese adults (24 participants each) examining food intake [13], a phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic study of single intravenous doses in overweight adults [14], a study of PYY degradation in healthy volunteers, and a trial of lingual PYY(3-36) on appetite and energy intake, with unknown status [5]. Published reports of infusion studies described reduced intake over a meal, as noted above [4][2]. No PYY product is approved for weight loss.
